passage: Naveen, five, burst through the door of their farmhouse near Amritsar, cap askew. "Papa Suraj Papa I saw a tractor with a huge tyre and it was going in the mud and the driver waved and the dog barked and I waved back and—" Suraj knelt, laughing. "Easy, easy. Tell me every part, one at a time." Naveen took a breath. "There was a... big tractor." "Yes?" "With a huge tyre. The driver waved." Suraj listened to each part, nodding, until the whole story unfolded.

qa.q: What did Naveen see with a huge tyre?
qa.a: He saw a tractor with a huge tyre going in the mud.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as his words tumbled out?
qa.a: He was excited and eager to share, and his words came in a rush with parts skipped. He may also have been afraid that Suraj would stop listening before the end.

qa.q: What worked in the way Suraj responded?
qa.a: He asked Naveen to tell every part one at a time and listened to each part, so Naveen could organise the story.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel as Naveen's story rushes out?
qa.a: He seems amused and fond, since he laughs, kneels and asks to hear every part, one at a time.

grounding: A preschooler with big news speaks in a rush, and a patient adult helps him organise his story.

passage: Ingrid, five, ran to the door of their Bergen flat. "Mamma, Rafael, at school we did a volcano and the red stuff came out and the teacher went back and the boy cried and it was so BIG—" Her brother Rafael, at the table with homework, grinned. "Wait, Ingrid. Start again." She took a breath. "We made a volcano." "And?" "The red stuff came out, and it went everywhere." She talked more slowly, and Rafael put his pencil down and said, "That's really cool."

qa.q: What did Ingrid's class make at school?
What was Ingrid feeling as she rushed through her news?
qa.a: She was very excited about the volcano and wanted to tell everything at once, so the words tumbled out. Her loud "BIG" suggests how much it thrilled her.

qa.q: What could Rafael do to help Ingrid tell her story?
qa.a: He can keep asking her to start again and prompt with short questions like "And?", as he did.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel about Ingrid's volcano news?
qa.a: He seems interested, since he puts his pencil down and says, "That's really cool."

grounding: A preschooler speaks in a rushed tumble when excited, and patient prompting helps her organise her story.
